script.opening: "I’ve had migraines for years, but now I’ve got a headache nearly every single day and the painkillers just aren’t working any more. I’m taking co-codamol most days and my migraine tablets too, and nothing touches it. Can you give me something stronger? I’m at the end of my tether."

facts.text: For about 4 months: a dull, pressing ache across the forehead most days, "there when I wake up". On top of that, proper migraines about 2 a week — one-sided throbbing, feel sick, can’t bear light or noise, have to lie down. "The bad ones still feel like my usual migraines."

If asked to count: co-codamol 30/500, two tablets "most mornings, sometimes twice a day" — about 20 days a month. Sumatriptan 50 mg on "maybe 12–15 days a month". Ibuprofen on top sometimes. "If I don’t take them first thing, it gets worse by lunchtime." Doesn’t keep a diary.

Never a sudden "worst ever" headache. No weakness, numbness, speech problems or confusion. No change in vision apart from the usual migraine zigzags before some attacks. Not worse lying down or on coughing; not woken by headache. No fever, rash, neck stiffness or weight loss. No head injury. "It’s the same type of headache, just all the time."
If asked: "The nurse did my blood pressure yesterday — she said it was fine." Had a routine eye test at the optician last month: "they said the backs of my eyes looked healthy."

Migraines since age 15, worse around periods. Tried propranolol years ago "for a few weeks — it made me tired so I stopped". Never tried anything else to prevent them. Not on the combined pill; uses the copper coil. Not pregnant, not planning pregnancy. No asthma. No allergies.

Works as a bank customer-service manager; has had 6 days off sick in 3 months and had a "return to work" meeting. Sleeping badly. Coffee about 5 mugs a day. Alcohol a glass of wine at weekends. Non-smoker. Lives with her partner, Dan. Mood "fed up and tearful sometimes" but no thoughts of harming herself if asked.

Tired, frustrated, near tears at times. You expect a stronger prescription. If told the painkillers are causing the headache, be disbelieving at first ("But they’re the only thing that helps"), then anxious about coping without them. Warm up if the doctor explains kindly, gives a clear plan, a preventer and follow-up. If simply given a stronger painkiller, accept it gratefully.

ice.ideas: "My migraines have just got worse — my body’s got used to the tablets so I need something stronger."
ice.concerns: "I’m scared it’s never going to stop, and I’ll lose my job if I keep having days off." Hidden worry, only if asked about worries: a colleague had a brain tumour, and she has secretly wondered about that.
ice.expectations: "Something stronger — maybe a stronger codeine, or an injection." Does not expect to be told to stop the tablets.

cues: "I’m taking co-codamol most days and my migraine tablets too" — counting the days reveals medication overuse.
"I’m at the end of my tether" — impact on work, sleep and mood worth exploring.
"A girl at work had a brain tumour…" (only if worries are explored) — the unspoken fear to address after the red-flag questions.

checkpoints.text: EXCLUDES secondary/red-flag headache FIRST (thunderclap, focal neurology/papilloedema/raised-ICP features, systemic features, substantial change in headache characteristics, GCA in older people — NICE CG150) before attributing to primary headache
Recognises MIGRAINE features and that the pattern has changed to near-daily, prompting the second diagnosis

Diagnoses MEDICATION-OVERUSE HEADACHE — near-daily headache with frequent acute analgesic/triptan use (triptans/opioids/combination ≥10 days/month or simple analgesics ≥15 days/month, >3 months) — and that the overused medication PERPETUATES it

Manages MOH by EXPLAINING the cycle and supporting WITHDRAWAL of the overused acute drug (NICE CG150: all overused acute drugs stopped abruptly for at least 1 month; specialist input if strong opioids; review at 4–8 weeks) with clear WARNING of transient worsening before improvement — not escalating analgesia

Optimises genuine migraine management — sparing acute treatment, PROPHYLAXIS (propranolol/amitriptyline/topiramate — topiramate only within the MHRA 2024 pregnancy prevention programme; candesartan off-label alt per BASH; riboflavin per CG150; aura and UKMEC checked), no opioids for acute migraine, triggers/sleep/lifestyle, headache diary
Responds compassionately to her desperation, explains why "something stronger" worsens MOH without sounding dismissive, and supports a difficult withdrawal plan
Sets realistic expectations (headache worsens transiently then improves), checks understanding, and agrees a shared plan with follow-up

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting urgent review (thunderclap, new neuro signs, systemic features), the withdrawal/prophylaxis plan with review, headache diary, and support — diagnosing and breaking the MOH cycle, not escalating painkillers

worked.txt: "I’m sorry it’s this relentless. First, a few safety checks: any sudden ‘worst-ever’ headaches, headaches worse in the morning or when lying down, vomiting, visual changes, weakness, or anything new and neurological? … No. Good — that’s reassuring."

"Here’s the thing that will sound counter-intuitive: I think the daily headache is now being driven by the painkillers themselves — it’s called medication-overuse headache. When you take acute painkillers or migraine tablets most days, they flip into causing a constant headache."

"So a stronger or more frequent painkiller is exactly the wrong move — it would deepen the problem. The way out is actually to come OFF the overused painkillers, which I know sounds frightening when you’re in pain."

"Let’s plan it together. We’ll stop the co-codamol and the migraine tablets completely for at least a month — all at once rather than cutting down, which works better. I have to be honest — your headache will likely get worse for a week or two before it gets better. That’s the medication clearing, it’s expected, and most people improve a lot afterwards."

"At the same time, let’s treat the underlying migraine properly — a daily preventer like propranolol or amitriptyline to reduce attacks, and afterwards keeping acute treatment — a triptan, with an anti-inflammatory or paracetamol if needed, not codeine — to fewer than 10 days a month, and a headache diary to spot triggers and track progress."

"I’ll review you through this, and properly at 4 to 8 weeks — you won’t be on your own. If you get a sudden severe headache, any weakness, vision or speech changes, or it’s simply not improving as expected, come back. We’re breaking a cycle here, and it does work."

f.learning: A near-daily headache in someone with a primary headache disorder who uses acute analgesics or triptans frequently is the picture of MEDICATION-OVERUSE HEADACHE (MOH), but the FIRST step is always to EXCLUDE secondary/red-flag headache: thunderclap onset (SAH), new focal neurology or raised-ICP/papilloedema features (morning headache, worse lying/Valsalva, vomiting), systemic features (fever, weight loss, immunosuppression, cancer history), a substantial change in the characteristics of the headache (NICE CG150), and GCA features in older patients. Recognise MIGRAINE (moderate-severe, often unilateral/throbbing, with nausea and photophobia/phonophobia, aggravated by activity, ± aura) and note when an episodic pattern has become near-daily. The key second diagnosis is MOH: a chronic daily/near-daily headache where triptans/opioids/combination analgesics are used on ≥10 days/month (or simple analgesics on ≥15 days/month) for over 3 months, with the OVERUSED MEDICATION now PERPETUATING the headache — so "something stronger" or more frequent painkillers makes it worse, and the diagnosis must be made rather than the analgesia escalated. Manage MOH by explaining the cycle and supporting WITHDRAWAL of the overused acute drug (NICE CG150: all overused acute drugs stopped abruptly, not gradually, for at least 1 month; specialist referral for strong-opioid overuse; review at 4–8 weeks), with a clear warning that the headache typically WORSENS for days-to-weeks before improving (expected and temporary), plus support and review. Simultaneously optimise migraine care — sparing acute treatment to avoid re-overuse, PROPHYLAXIS where frequent (propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate — noting topiramate’s teratogenicity, the MHRA 2024 pregnancy prevention programme and reduced contraceptive efficacy; candesartan as an off-label alternative per BASH; riboflavin 400 mg daily may help per CG150; no opioids for acute migraine, CG150; ask about aura, UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception), trigger/sleep/lifestyle measures and a headache diary. The hidden agenda is the desperate wish for a stronger painkiller; explain compassionately why that worsens MOH, support a realistic withdrawal plan, and safety-net for red flags.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG150 (headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management, 2012, updated June 2025) · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2024 (topiramate: pregnancy prevention programme) · [3] British Association for the Study of Headache (BASH) National headache management system for adults (2019) · [4] UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (CoSRH UKMEC 2025)
knowledge.summary: Long-standing migraine that has become near-daily, with co-codamol and a triptan taken on most days, is medication-overuse headache on top of migraine until proved otherwise. The painkillers are now keeping the headache going, so ‘something stronger’ would make it worse. Exclude secondary headache, then withdraw the overused drugs with a warning about the short-term worsening, start a preventer, and review.

points.t: NICE CG150 [1] lists features needing further investigation or referral, including: sudden onset reaching maximum within 5 minutes; new neurological deficit or cognitive change; personality change; impaired consciousness; headache with fever; headache triggered by cough, Valsalva, sneeze or exercise; orthostatic headache; symptoms of giant cell arteritis or acute angle-closure glaucoma; head injury in the last 3 months; and a substantial change in the character of the headache. Check blood pressure and fundi.

NICE CG150 [1]: be alert to medication-overuse headache in people with headache on 15 days a month or more who have taken triptans, opioids, ergots or combination analgesics on 10 days a month or more, or paracetamol, aspirin or an NSAID on 15 days a month or more, for 3 months or more. Co-codamol counts as an opioid and a combination analgesic.

NICE CG150 [1]: explain that it is treated by withdrawing the overused medication; advise stopping all overused acute headache drugs for at least 1 month, abruptly rather than gradually; warn that headache is likely to get worse in the short term and that withdrawal symptoms may occur; provide close follow-up; consider specialist referral for people using strong opioids or with relevant comorbidities. Review the diagnosis and management 4–8 weeks after withdrawal starts.

NICE CG150 [1]: do not offer ergots or opioids for the acute treatment of migraine. After withdrawal, the acute plan is a triptan with or without an NSAID or paracetamol, limited to fewer than 10 days a month.

NICE CG150 [1] and BASH [3]: consider a preventer when attacks are frequent or disabling. Options include propranolol, amitriptyline and topiramate; candesartan is used off-label (BASH [3]). Titrate to an effective dose and judge after an adequate trial. CG150 [1] also advises that riboflavin 400 mg once a day may reduce frequency and intensity for some people. Doses per BNF.

MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2024 [2]: topiramate is teratogenic and must not be used for migraine prevention in pregnancy, nor in women who could become pregnant unless the pregnancy prevention programme conditions are met. It can reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, so ask about contraception and pregnancy plans before choosing any preventer.
UKMEC [4]: migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception at any age. Ask about aura and current contraception at a headache review.

Refer if red flags, diagnostic doubt, strong-opioid use, failure of withdrawal, or failure of adequate trials of preventers. Specialist-only options include botulinum toxin type A for chronic migraine (NICE TA260) and CGRP monoclonal antibodies after three failed preventers (for example NICE TA764, fremanezumab).

dg.d: Open question; let her finish the request for ‘something stronger’ and acknowledged the toll first.
Explored the impact on her life and her fear it will never stop; checked what matters before planning.
Reviews the recorded blood pressure and optometrist’s fundoscopy; screens neurological symptoms (in-person examination if any); headache and medication diary.
Migraine with superimposed medication-overuse headache versus secondary headache; tested with the CG150 red-flag list.
Screened thunderclap, raised-pressure features, neurological deficit, fever, cough or exertion triggers; recorded BP and fundi normal, no neurological symptoms.
Medication-overuse headache: opioid or combination analgesic and triptan on most days for months (CG150 thresholds).
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Abrupt withdrawal of all overused drugs for at least 1 month with warning; preventer started; opioid off repeat; acute plan under 10 days a month.
Checked asthma before propranolol, contraception and pregnancy plans before any preventer (topiramate MHRA 2024).
Review at 2 weeks and within 4–8 weeks of starting withdrawal; teach-back; specific red flags.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up ‘nothing touches it’ and daily use of two acute drugs as the cue to count medication days.
Idea: migraines worse, needs stronger drug. Concern: it will never stop. Expectation: stronger painkiller.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I’m scared it’s never going to stop, and I’ll lose my job if I keep having days off." Hidden worry, only if asked about worries: a colleague had a brain tumour, and she has secretly wondered about that — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Miss Page, I’m Dr Evans. Thanks for joining the video call. What’s been happening?

I’ve had migraines for years, but now I’ve got a headache nearly every single day and the painkillers aren’t working any more. I’m taking co-codamol most days and my migraine tablets too. Can you give me something stronger? I’m at the end of my tether.

That sounds exhausting — a headache nearly every day would wear anyone down. I do want to help you get out of this. Can I ask some questions first, check a few things, and then we’ll work out a plan together?
model.why: Empathy first, then a clear agenda

model.text: Please. Anything.
Tell me about the headaches now compared with your usual migraines. Is it the same kind of headache, just more often, or something new?
The bad ones still feel like migraines. In between it’s a duller headache that’s just always there.
How long has it been nearly every day? And roughly how many days a month do you take co-codamol, and how many the migraine tablets?
model.why: Counts headache days and acute-medication days against the CG150 thresholds

model.text: A few months now. Co-codamol most days. The migraine tablets most days as well.

Thank you — that helps a lot. Some safety questions I ask everyone. Has any headache come on suddenly, like a thunderclap? Is it worse lying down or in the morning, or with coughing or straining? Any weakness, numbness, changes in vision or speech, fever, or feeling muddled?
No, nothing like that. Same pattern, just all the time.

Good. The nurse checked your blood pressure yesterday and the optometrist looked at the backs of your eyes last month — can I go through those with you, and ask a few quick questions about your nerves?
model.why: Reviews recorded BP and fundoscopy; screens neurological symptoms

model.text: Yes, fine.

(reviewing the recorded findings) Your blood pressure was normal and the optometrist found the backs of your eyes healthy, with no sign of raised pressure. And you’ve no weakness, numbness, double vision or problems with balance or speech. That’s reassuring.
model.why: Shares normal findings to support a primary headache diagnosis

model.text: What have you been thinking is going on? And what worries you most?
That my migraines have got worse and I need something stronger. I’m scared it’ll never stop. It’s taking over my life.

I can hear how much this is costing you. I’m going to say something that sounds back to front, so bear with me. I think your daily headache is now being caused by the painkillers themselves. It’s called medication-overuse headache. When codeine or migraine tablets are taken on most days for months, the brain becomes more sensitive and a daily headache sets in.
model.why: Names medication-overuse headache and explains the mechanism simply

model.text: So the tablets are making it worse? But they’re the only thing that helps.

They give a little relief for a few hours, and then the headache comes back, so you take more. That’s the cycle. Something stronger would deepen it. The way out is to stop the tablets that are being overused. I know that’s frightening to hear when you’re in pain.
model.why: Explains why ‘stronger’ would harm, without dismissing her

model.text: (quietly) I really don’t know if I can do that.
You won’t be doing it alone. Let me show you what the plan looks like, and you tell me what feels possible.
model.why: Responds to her fear and invites partnership

model.text: The advice is to stop both the co-codamol and the migraine tablets completely for at least a month — all at once rather than slowly. I must be honest: for a week or two the headache usually gets worse, and you may feel a bit rough, before it gets better. That’s the medicine clearing, not a sign it’s failing.
model.why: NICE CG150 withdrawal advice with an honest warning about short-term worsening

model.text: A worse headache for two weeks? How do I get through that?

We start a daily preventer now so it’s working underneath. Propranolol or amitriptyline are the usual first choices — both reduce how often migraines come. Before we pick, I need to check a few things: any asthma, and your contraception and pregnancy plans, because some preventers aren’t safe in pregnancy. And we’ll keep a headache diary so we can both see progress.
model.why: Starts prophylaxis, checks contraindications and contraception, uses a diary

model.text: Okay. And after the month?

Then we rebuild a proper plan for migraine attacks — a triptan, maybe with an anti-inflammatory, used early, but on fewer than ten days a month. Codeine isn’t a good migraine treatment, so we’ll take it off your repeat. I’ll see you in two weeks to see how you’re coping, and again at around six weeks to review everything.
model.why: Acute plan within limits; opioid removed; follow-up within the CG150 4–8 week review window

model.text: That’s more than I expected. I thought you’d just give me a prescription.
Can you tell me back the plan in your own words, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Stop the co-codamol and migraine tablets for a month. It’ll be worse for a week or two. Start a preventer. Keep a diary. Back in two weeks.

Perfect. If you get a sudden, severe headache that peaks within minutes, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or seeing, fever with a stiff neck, or feel confused, seek urgent help the same day — 999 for the sudden severe one. And if you’re struggling before two weeks, call us.
model.why: Specific red-flag safety net and an open door

model.text: Thank you. I actually feel hopeful for once.

social.t: Chronic daily headache affects work, sleep and mood. Ask about low mood and how she is coping; amitriptyline may suit if sleep is poor, but treat any depression in its own right.
Daily codeine for months can cause withdrawal symptoms. Explain this openly and without judgement, and offer more support if stopping proves hard.

legal.t: Migraine that has a substantial and long-term effect on day-to-day activities can count as a disability, giving a right to reasonable adjustments at work. A fit note can advise adjustments if work is affected.

professional.t: Review repeat opioid prescriptions and remove co-codamol from repeat for migraine (NICE CG150: do not offer opioids for acute migraine). Document the reason and the plan.
MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2024: topiramate for migraine prevention requires the pregnancy prevention programme in anyone who could become pregnant. Record the discussion if it is ever chosen.

community.t: The Migraine Trust and National Migraine Centre offer information and headache diaries; community pharmacists can reinforce the medication-day limits.

redFlags: Thunderclap onset, new neurological deficit, confusion, fever with neck stiffness — same-day assessment
Headache worse lying down or on waking with vomiting, or triggered by cough or exertion
Substantial change in headache character, or symptoms of GCA or angle-closure glaucoma
psychosocial: Impact on work, sleep, mood and daily life
Fear it will never stop; exhaustion
Contraception, pregnancy plans, asthma — shape the preventer choice
ice: Idea: migraines have worsened; needs something stronger
Concern: a headache that never stops; being out of control

playbook.diagnosis: Medication-overuse headache superimposed on long-standing migraine: near-daily headache for months with co-codamol and triptan on most days (above the NICE CG150 threshold of 10 days a month). No red flags; recorded BP and fundi normal, no neurological symptoms.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The painkillers and migraine tablets, taken on most days, have started causing a daily headache of their own. Stopping them breaks the cycle — it gets worse for a short time, then much better.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for something stronger because you’re desperate. I understand — but stronger would keep you stuck, and there is a way out.”
management.psychosocial: Support her through withdrawal with early contact; ask about mood and work; involve her in choosing the preventer.
sharedPlan: Stop co-codamol and triptan abruptly for at least 1 month; warn of 1–2 weeks of worsening (NICE CG150)
Start a preventer (propranolol or amitriptyline first, after checking asthma, contraception and pregnancy plans); headache diary
After withdrawal: triptan with or without NSAID, early in an attack, on fewer than 10 days a month; no opioids
Review at 2 weeks and again 4–8 weeks after withdrawal starts
safetyNet: Sudden severe headache, weakness, speech or vision change, fever with stiff neck, confusion — urgent same-day help, 999 for thunderclap
Call before the review if she cannot cope with withdrawal

pitfalls.intro: This station rewards the doctor who turns down the request for a stronger drug and still leaves the patient feeling helped. It is failed by prescribing, by preaching, or by a withdrawal plan with no support.

items.fail: Prescribing a stronger opioid or an extra triptan.
items.why: Escalation deepens medication-overuse headache; NICE CG150 advises against opioids for migraine.
items.fix: Diagnose medication-overuse headache and plan withdrawal.

items.fail: Diagnosing medication-overuse headache without a red-flag screen or checking the examination findings.
items.why: Secondary headache must be excluded first.
items.fix: Run the CG150 red-flag questions and check BP, fundi and neurology.

items.fail: “Try to cut down the co-codamol slowly.”
items.why: NICE CG150 advises stopping all overused drugs abruptly for at least a month; specialist referral is for strong opioids.
items.fix: Stop both overused drugs, warn about worsening, and follow up closely.

items.fail: Starting topiramate with no contraception or pregnancy discussion.
items.why: MHRA June 2024: topiramate needs the pregnancy prevention programme and reduces hormonal contraceptive effect.
items.fix: Ask first; propranolol or amitriptyline are usual first choices.

items.fail: Telling her she is ‘addicted’ or ‘taking far too many tablets’.
items.why: Blame makes her defensive and less likely to succeed.
items.fix: Explain the cycle as a common trap and offer support.

items.fail: No warning that the headache will worsen before it improves.
items.why: Without the warning she will restart the tablets in the first week.
items.fix: Warn clearly and book an early check-in.

items.why: CG150 asks for review 4–8 weeks after withdrawal starts.
items.fix: Book a 2-week contact and a 4–8 week review.

SCA_MODELS.text: What have you been thinking is going on? And what worries you most?
That my migraines have got worse and I need something stronger. I’m scared it’ll never stop. It’s taking over my life.

I can hear how much this is costing you. I’m going to say something that sounds back to front, so bear with me. I think your daily headache is now being caused by the painkillers themselves. It’s called medication-overuse headache. When codeine or migraine tablets are taken on most days for months, the brain becomes more sensitive and a daily headache sets in.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names medication-overuse headache and explains the mechanism simply

SCA_MODELS.text: So the tablets are making it worse? But they’re the only thing that helps.

They give a little relief for a few hours, and then the headache comes back, so you take more. That’s the cycle. Something stronger would deepen it. The way out is to stop the tablets that are being overused. I know that’s frightening to hear when you’re in pain.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why ‘stronger’ would harm, without dismissing her

SCA_MODELS.text: (quietly) I really don’t know if I can do that.
You won’t be doing it alone. Let me show you what the plan looks like, and you tell me what feels possible.
SCA_MODELS.why: Responds to her fear and invites partnership

SCA_MODELS.text: The advice is to stop both the co-codamol and the migraine tablets completely for at least a month — all at once rather than slowly. I must be honest: for a week or two the headache usually gets worse, and you may feel a bit rough, before it gets better. That’s the medicine clearing, not a sign it’s failing.
SCA_MODELS.why: NICE CG150 withdrawal advice with an honest warning about short-term worsening

SCA_MODELS.text: A worse headache for two weeks? How do I get through that?

We start a daily preventer now so it’s working underneath. Propranolol or amitriptyline are the usual first choices — both reduce how often migraines come. Before we pick, I need to check a few things: any asthma, and your contraception and pregnancy plans, because some preventers aren’t safe in pregnancy. And we’ll keep a headache diary so we can both see progress.
SCA_MODELS.why: Starts prophylaxis, checks contraindications and contraception, uses a diary

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. And after the month?

Then we rebuild a proper plan for migraine attacks — a triptan, maybe with an anti-inflammatory, used early, but on fewer than ten days a month. Codeine isn’t a good migraine treatment, so we’ll take it off your repeat. I’ll see you in two weeks to see how you’re coping, and again at around six weeks to review everything.
SCA_MODELS.why: Acute plan within limits; opioid removed; follow-up within the CG150 4–8 week review window

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s more than I expected. I thought you’d just give me a prescription.
Can you tell me back the plan in your own words, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Stop the co-codamol and migraine tablets for a month. It’ll be worse for a week or two. Start a preventer. Keep a diary. Back in two weeks.

Perfect. If you get a sudden, severe headache that peaks within minutes, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or seeing, fever with a stiff neck, or feel confused, seek urgent help the same day — 999 for the sudden severe one. And if you’re struggling before two weeks, call us.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific red-flag safety net and an open door

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. I actually feel hopeful for once.

SCA_STEM.name: Rowena Page
pmh: Migraine for many years (episodic until recently)
meds: Triptan (acute migraine treatment) — taking most days
SCA_STEM.recent: Headache now nearly every day. Frequent requests for co-codamol and triptan on the repeat record. No headache diary on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation. “Nothing touches it — can I have something stronger?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG150 (headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management, 2012, updated June 2025) · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2024 (topiramate: pregnancy prevention programme) · [3] British Association for the Study of Headache (BASH) National headache management system for adults (2019) · [4] UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (CoSRH UKMEC 2025)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Long-standing migraine that has become near-daily, with co-codamol and a triptan taken on most days, is medication-overuse headache on top of migraine until proved otherwise. The painkillers are now keeping the headache going, so ‘something stronger’ would make it worse. Exclude secondary headache, then withdraw the overused drugs with a warning about the short-term worsening, start a preventer, and review.

points.t: NICE CG150 [1] lists features needing further investigation or referral, including: sudden onset reaching maximum within 5 minutes; new neurological deficit or cognitive change; personality change; impaired consciousness; headache with fever; headache triggered by cough, Valsalva, sneeze or exercise; orthostatic headache; symptoms of giant cell arteritis or acute angle-closure glaucoma; head injury in the last 3 months; and a substantial change in the character of the headache. Check blood pressure and fundi.

NICE CG150 [1]: be alert to medication-overuse headache in people with headache on 15 days a month or more who have taken triptans, opioids, ergots or combination analgesics on 10 days a month or more, or paracetamol, aspirin or an NSAID on 15 days a month or more, for 3 months or more. Co-codamol counts as an opioid and a combination analgesic.

NICE CG150 [1]: explain that it is treated by withdrawing the overused medication; advise stopping all overused acute headache drugs for at least 1 month, abruptly rather than gradually; warn that headache is likely to get worse in the short term and that withdrawal symptoms may occur; provide close follow-up; consider specialist referral for people using strong opioids or with relevant comorbidities. Review the diagnosis and management 4–8 weeks after withdrawal starts.

NICE CG150 [1]: do not offer ergots or opioids for the acute treatment of migraine. After withdrawal, the acute plan is a triptan with or without an NSAID or paracetamol, limited to fewer than 10 days a month.

NICE CG150 [1] and BASH [3]: consider a preventer when attacks are frequent or disabling. Options include propranolol, amitriptyline and topiramate; candesartan is used off-label (BASH [3]). Titrate to an effective dose and judge after an adequate trial. CG150 [1] also advises that riboflavin 400 mg once a day may reduce frequency and intensity for some people. Doses per BNF.

MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2024 [2]: topiramate is teratogenic and must not be used for migraine prevention in pregnancy, nor in women who could become pregnant unless the pregnancy prevention programme conditions are met. It can reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, so ask about contraception and pregnancy plans before choosing any preventer.
UKMEC [4]: migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception at any age. Ask about aura and current contraception at a headache review.

Refer if red flags, diagnostic doubt, strong-opioid use, failure of withdrawal, or failure of adequate trials of preventers. Specialist-only options include botulinum toxin type A for chronic migraine (NICE TA260) and CGRP monoclonal antibodies after three failed preventers (for example NICE TA764, fremanezumab).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her finish the request for ‘something stronger’ and acknowledged the toll first.
Explored the impact on her life and her fear it will never stop; checked what matters before planning.
Picked up ‘nothing touches it’ and daily use of two acute drugs as the cue to count medication days.
Idea: migraines worse, needs stronger drug. Concern: it will never stop. Expectation: stronger painkiller.
Reviews the recorded blood pressure and optometrist’s fundoscopy; screens neurological symptoms (in-person examination if any); headache and medication diary.
Migraine with superimposed medication-overuse headache versus secondary headache; tested with the CG150 red-flag list.
Screened thunderclap, raised-pressure features, neurological deficit, fever, cough or exertion triggers; recorded BP and fundi normal, no neurological symptoms.
Medication-overuse headache: opioid or combination analgesic and triptan on most days for months (CG150 thresholds).
Abrupt withdrawal of all overused drugs for at least 1 month with warning; preventer started; opioid off repeat; acute plan under 10 days a month.
Checked asthma before propranolol, contraception and pregnancy plans before any preventer (topiramate MHRA 2024).
Review at 2 weeks and within 4–8 weeks of starting withdrawal; teach-back; specific red flags.

social.t: Chronic daily headache affects work, sleep and mood. Ask about low mood and how she is coping; amitriptyline may suit if sleep is poor, but treat any depression in its own right.
Daily codeine for months can cause withdrawal symptoms. Explain this openly and without judgement, and offer more support if stopping proves hard.

legal.t: Migraine that has a substantial and long-term effect on day-to-day activities can count as a disability, giving a right to reasonable adjustments at work. A fit note can advise adjustments if work is affected.

professional.t: Review repeat opioid prescriptions and remove co-codamol from repeat for migraine (NICE CG150: do not offer opioids for acute migraine). Document the reason and the plan.
MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2024: topiramate for migraine prevention requires the pregnancy prevention programme in anyone who could become pregnant. Record the discussion if it is ever chosen.

community.t: The Migraine Trust and National Migraine Centre offer information and headache diaries; community pharmacists can reinforce the medication-day limits.

redFlags: Thunderclap onset, new neurological deficit, confusion, fever with neck stiffness — same-day assessment
Headache worse lying down or on waking with vomiting, or triggered by cough or exertion
Substantial change in headache character, or symptoms of GCA or angle-closure glaucoma
psychosocial: Impact on work, sleep, mood and daily life
Fear it will never stop; exhaustion
Contraception, pregnancy plans, asthma — shape the preventer choice
ice: Idea: migraines have worsened; needs something stronger
Concern: a headache that never stops; being out of control

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Medication-overuse headache superimposed on long-standing migraine: near-daily headache for months with co-codamol and triptan on most days (above the NICE CG150 threshold of 10 days a month). No red flags; recorded BP and fundi normal, no neurological symptoms.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The painkillers and migraine tablets, taken on most days, have started causing a daily headache of their own. Stopping them breaks the cycle — it gets worse for a short time, then much better.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for something stronger because you’re desperate. I understand — but stronger would keep you stuck, and there is a way out.”
management.psychosocial: Support her through withdrawal with early contact; ask about mood and work; involve her in choosing the preventer.
sharedPlan: Stop co-codamol and triptan abruptly for at least 1 month; warn of 1–2 weeks of worsening (NICE CG150)
Start a preventer (propranolol or amitriptyline first, after checking asthma, contraception and pregnancy plans); headache diary
After withdrawal: triptan with or without NSAID, early in an attack, on fewer than 10 days a month; no opioids
Review at 2 weeks and again 4–8 weeks after withdrawal starts
safetyNet: Sudden severe headache, weakness, speech or vision change, fever with stiff neck, confusion — urgent same-day help, 999 for thunderclap
Call before the review if she cannot cope with withdrawal

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station rewards the doctor who turns down the request for a stronger drug and still leaves the patient feeling helped. It is failed by prescribing, by preaching, or by a withdrawal plan with no support.

items.fail: Prescribing a stronger opioid or an extra triptan.
items.why: Escalation deepens medication-overuse headache; NICE CG150 advises against opioids for migraine.
items.fix: Diagnose medication-overuse headache and plan withdrawal.

items.fail: Diagnosing medication-overuse headache without a red-flag screen or checking the examination findings.
items.why: Secondary headache must be excluded first.
items.fix: Run the CG150 red-flag questions and check BP, fundi and neurology.

items.fail: “Try to cut down the co-codamol slowly.”
items.why: NICE CG150 advises stopping all overused drugs abruptly for at least a month; specialist referral is for strong opioids.
items.fix: Stop both overused drugs, warn about worsening, and follow up closely.

items.fail: Starting topiramate with no contraception or pregnancy discussion.
items.why: MHRA June 2024: topiramate needs the pregnancy prevention programme and reduces hormonal contraceptive effect.
items.fix: Ask first; propranolol or amitriptyline are usual first choices.

items.fail: Telling her she is ‘addicted’ or ‘taking far too many tablets’.
items.why: Blame makes her defensive and less likely to succeed.
items.fix: Explain the cycle as a common trap and offer support.

items.fail: No warning that the headache will worsen before it improves.
items.why: Without the warning she will restart the tablets in the first week.
items.fix: Warn clearly and book an early check-in.

items.why: CG150 asks for review 4–8 weeks after withdrawal starts.
items.fix: Book a 2-week contact and a 4–8 week review.
